newsitem.title: USA: Study shows secondhand smoke doubles risk - NYT.
newsitem.headline: Study shows secondhand smoke doubles risk - NYT.

text.p: A 10-year study conducted by Harvard University researchers shows that secondhand smoke doubles a person's risk of heart disease, the New York Times said.

In its Tuesday edition, the Times said the study tracked more than 32,000 healthy women who never smoked but who were regularly exposed to other people's smoke at home or in the office. Its findings are to be released on Tuesday.
The Times said the study's findings indicate that secondhand smoke is more dangerous than previously thought.
The women in the study, who ranged in age from 36 to 61 when the study began, suffered 152 heart attacks, 25 of them fatal.

Those results mean that "there may be up to 50,000 Americans dying of heart attacks from passive smoke each year," said Dr. Ichiro Kawachi, an assistant professor of health and social behaviour at the Harvard School of Public Health and the lead author of the study.
In contrast, deaths from lung cancer as a result of passive smoking are estimated to be far fewer, at 3,000 to 4,000 annually.
The study may be used in some of the pending lawsuits against tobacco companies.
"From our standpoint, that's a wonderful study," said Stanley Rosenblatt, a Miami lawyer representing flight attendants in a class-action lawsuit against tobacco companies.
That lawsuit is based on the effects of secondhand smoke.
The Times said that Philip Morris Cos Inc, a defendant in the flight-attendants' lawsuit, declined to comment, as did the Tobacco Institute, an industry group.
